topics.name: Rules and the nature of law

cards: Laws are rules enforced by the state with sanctions; rules include moral, religious and social norms.
Law and morality overlap (e.g. murder) but differ. Hart-Devlin debate on whether law should enforce morality.
Justice theories: Aristotle (distributive and corrective), utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill) and Marxist views.
Law balances competing interests (Pound) and maintains social control.
Liability usually depends on fault, but strict liability offences don't need it.
Statute law (Acts of Parliament), delegated legislation, common law (judicial precedent) and retained EU law.
Criminal law: the state prosecutes; burden of proof on the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt. Civil law: disputes between individuals; balance of probabilities.
Natural law: law should follow moral principles. Positivism: law is valid if made correctly, regardless of morality.
Dicey: no punishment except for a breach of law; equality before the law; rights protected by courts.
Green and White Papers, readings, committee stage, report stage, royal assent. Parliament is sovereign.
Dicey: Parliament can make or unmake any law and no Parliament can bind its successors.
Statutory instruments, by-laws and Orders in Council made under an enabling Act. Controlled by affirmative and negative resolutions and judicial review.
Literal rule (plain meaning, e.g. Whiteley v Chappell), golden rule (avoid absurdity, Adler v George), mischief rule (Smith v Hughes), purposive approach.
Intrinsic (the Act itself) and extrinsic (Hansard after Pepper v Hart, dictionaries, Law Commission reports).
Stare decisis: lower courts follow higher courts' ratio decidendi. Obiter dicta are persuasive.
Overruling, distinguishing, reversing, and the Practice Statement 1966 allowing the Supreme Court to depart from its own decisions.
Law Commission proposals, judicial changes and pressure groups.
Saves parliamentary time, uses expertise and local knowledge, and can be made quickly.
Lack of democratic involvement, too much made to be properly scrutinised, and sub-delegation.
Supreme Court, Court of Appeal, High Court, then lower courts. Each follows courts above it.
Respects parliamentary sovereignty and is predictable, but can give absurd results.
Heydon's case: judges look for the mischief the Act was passed to remedy and interpret accordingly.
Judges look for Parliament's purpose, used more since EU membership; criticised for judicial law-making.
Original precedent: a new point of law. Persuasive precedent: decisions from lower courts, other jurisdictions or obiter dicta.
County Court and High Court; small claims, fast track and multi-track; appeals to the Court of Appeal.
Negotiation, mediation, conciliation and arbitration; cheaper and quicker than court.
Magistrates' Court (summary offences), Crown Court (indictable offences) with juries. Appeals to the Court of Appeal.
Magistrates (unpaid, local) and juries (randomly selected). Advantages: public participation. Disadvantages: inconsistency, lack of legal knowledge.
Solicitors and barristers; training routes and regulation by the SRA and BSB.
Superior and inferior judges; independence protected by security of tenure and the Constitutional Reform Act 2005.
Legal aid (LASPO 2012 cut civil legal aid), conditional fee agreements and advice agencies.
Aged 18-65, good character, sit at least 13 days a year, and assisted by a legal adviser.
Aged 18-75, on the electoral register, randomly selected; some people are disqualified.
Public confidence and jury equity vs lack of reasons, possible bias and media influence.
Punishment, reduction of crime (deterrence), reform and rehabilitation, protection of the public and reparation.
Custodial, community orders, fines and discharges.
Specialist bodies resolving disputes, e.g. employment tribunals; cheaper and quicker than courts.
The guilty act: a voluntary act, omission (where there is a duty, e.g. Pittwood, Stone and Dobinson) or state of affairs.
Factual causation: 'but for' test (White). Legal causation: operating and substantial cause (Smith), thin skull rule (Blaue) and no novus actus interveniens.
Intention (direct and oblique - Woollin: virtual certainty) or recklessness (Cunningham subjective test).
Offences needing no mens rea for part of the actus reus, e.g. Harrow LBC v Shah; often regulatory.
Mens rea transfers to a different victim (Latimer). Actus reus and mens rea must coincide (Fagan, Thabo Meli).
No general duty to act, but duties exist by contract (Pittwood), relationship (Gibbins and Proctor), voluntary assumption (Stone and Dobinson), statute and creating a danger (Miller).
A new intervening act breaks the chain of causation, e.g. third-party actions (Pagett), medical treatment that is 'palpably wrong' (Jordan), or the victim's unreasonable act (Roberts).
The defendant's aim or purpose is to bring about the consequence (Mohan).
The unlawful killing of a human being under the Queen's (King's) peace with malice aforethought: intention to kill or cause GBH (Vickers).

Partial defence (Coroners and Justice Act 2009): loss of self-control, a qualifying trigger (fear of serious violence or circumstances of an extremely grave character) and a person of the defendant's sex and age would act similarly.
Partial defence: abnormality of mental functioning from a recognised medical condition that substantially impaired the defendant's ability and explains the killing.
An unlawful and dangerous act that causes death (Church: dangerous to a reasonable person). Mens rea of the unlawful act needed.
Adomako test: duty of care, breach, causing death, and negligence so gross it is criminal.
Woollin: the jury may find intention if death or serious injury was a virtual certainty and the defendant appreciated that.
Mandatory life sentence, with a minimum term set by the judge.
Law Commission proposed a three-tier structure of first-degree murder, second-degree murder and manslaughter.
Church: would a sober and reasonable person realise the act carries a risk of some physical harm?
Causing the victim to apprehend immediate unlawful force (Ireland, Constanza). Mens rea: intention or recklessness.
Application of unlawful force (Collins v Wilcock). Can be indirect (Haystead).
Assault or battery causing actual bodily harm (Miller: any hurt or injury; Chan-Fook: psychiatric injury). Mens rea of assault or battery only (Savage).
Unlawful wounding (breaking the skin, Eisenhower) or inflicting grievous bodily harm (really serious harm, Smith). Mens rea: foresight of some harm (Mowatt).
Wounding or causing GBH with intent to cause GBH or resist arrest. Maximum life sentence.
The 1861 Act is outdated and inconsistent; the Law Commission proposed a new Act in 2015.
Covers s47 ABH, s20 GBH and s18 GBH with intent; assault and battery are under s39 Criminal Justice Act 1988.
Recognised psychiatric injury can be ABH or GBH (Chan-Fook, Burstow).
Requires both layers of skin to be broken (JCC v Eisenhower).
Dishonest appropriation of property belonging to another with intention to permanently deprive (Theft Act 1968 s1).
Ivey v Genting test (2017): what was the defendant's genuine belief, and was it dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people?
Theft with force or threat of force immediately before or at the time, in order to steal (s8).
Assuming the rights of the owner (s3), even with consent (Gomez).
Property in the possession or control of another, or someone with a proprietary interest (s5).
Treating the property as one's own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights (s6), e.g. borrowing until value is lost (Lloyd).
M'Naghten Rules: defect of reason from a disease of the mind, so the defendant didn't know the nature of the act or that it was wrong. Special verdict.
Insane automatism (internal cause) vs non-insane automatism (external cause, e.g. a blow to the head). Self-induced automatism may not be a defence.
Voluntary intoxication is a defence only to specific intent crimes (Majewski). Involuntary intoxication can be a defence if no mens rea (Kingston).
Force must be necessary and reasonable in the circumstances as the defendant believed them to be. Householder cases allow force that isn't grossly disproportionate.
By threats or circumstances: threat of death or serious injury, sober person of reasonable firmness would act the same (Graham). Not a defence to murder (Howe).
A defence to assault and battery; not usually to ABH or above (Brown), with exceptions such as sports and surgery.
Criminal Attempts Act 1981: an act more than merely preparatory with intent to commit the offence.
Duress of circumstances: Re A (conjoined twins) allowed necessity in exceptional circumstances.
An honest mistaken belief can negate mens rea or support self-defence, unless caused by voluntary intoxication.
Duress is unavailable if the defendant voluntarily joined a criminal gang knowing they might be threatened (Hasan).
Caparo test: foreseeability of damage, proximity and fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty. Donoghue v Stevenson neighbour principle.
The defendant falls below the standard of a reasonable person. Factors: special characteristics, risk, precautions and social benefit (Bolton v Stone, Bolam).
Factual causation ('but for', Barnett) and remoteness (reasonable foreseeability, The Wagon Mound).
1957 Act to lawful visitors: common duty of care. 1984 Act to trespassers: duty if the occupier knows of the danger and a trespasser may come near it.
Unreasonable interference with a person's use or enjoyment of land. Factors: locality, duration, sensitivity and malice.
Strict liability for escape of something likely to cause damage brought onto land for non-natural use.
An employer is liable for torts committed by employees in the course of employment (Mohamud v Morrison).
Contributory negligence (reduces damages), consent (volenti non fit injuria).
Compensatory damages and injunctions. Damages aim to put the claimant in the position as if the tort hadn't occurred.
'The thing speaks for itself': breach is inferred when the accident would not normally happen without negligence.
Primary victims (in danger) and secondary victims (Alcock criteria: close tie of love and affection, proximity in time and space, saw it with their own senses).
Generally not recoverable, except negligent misstatement (Hedley Byrne).
Occupiers must expect children to be less careful (Glasgow Corporation v Taylor).
Statutory authority and prescription (20 years); coming to the nuisance is not a defence.
Claimants must take reasonable steps to reduce their losses.
An offer is a definite promise to be bound. Adverts and goods on display are usually invitations to treat (Fisher v Bell, Partridge v Crittenden).
Must mirror the offer. Postal rule: acceptance is effective when posted (Adams v Lindsell).
Something of value given in exchange; must be sufficient but needn't be adequate; past consideration is not valid.
Presumed in commercial agreements; not in domestic ones unless shown otherwise (Balfour v Balfour).
Express and implied terms. Conditions, warranties and innominate terms. Consumer Rights Act 2015 implies terms of quality and fitness.
A false statement of fact inducing a contract. Can be fraudulent, negligent or innocent.
By performance, frustration or breach. Remedies include damages, rescission and specific performance.
An offer can be revoked before acceptance, communicated by the offeror or a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds).
Accepted by performing the act requested (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co).
Only parties to a contract can enforce it, but the Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 allows exceptions.
Must be incorporated and are controlled by the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977.
A contract becomes impossible, illegal or radically different through no fault of either party (Taylor v Caldwell).
